screens.title: VHDL for Combinational and Sequential Logic
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn the two fundamental ways VHDL models hardware: concurrent statements that behave like physical wires and sequential statements inside processes that behave like small programs driven by events. You will see how simple concurrent signal assignments map directly to combinational gates, how conditional and selected assignments express multiplexing cleanly, and how processes use sensitivity lists and clock-edge checks to implement registers and finite state machines. We will practice counters, synchronous reset patterns, and a state-machine design that uses an enumerated type for readable states. You will also observe the important difference between signals and variables inside a process: signals update after the process completes, while variables update immediately and are useful for temporary calculations. These patterns are essential for synthesizable, maintainable HDL. By the end you'll be able to choose the correct VHDL construct for combinational logic versus sequential logic and reason about timing and synthesis implications. Think about a design you might write: will the behavior be expressed as parallel wiring or as time-driven state updates?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical VHDL skills you will practice. First, you will use concurrent signal assignments and the conditional select forms to express combinational logic concisely and in a way that synthesizes to gates and multiplexers. For example, you will write a conditional assignment that selects one of four inputs based on a two-bit selector. Second, you will write processes with full sensitivity lists to model combinational behavior and understand why listing every input matters. This helps avoid accidental latches and ensures predictable synthesis. Third, you will implement registers, counters, and finite state machines with clock-edge detection and synchronous reset patterns so your design updates only on clock edges. You will code a counter that increments under enable and resets with others => '0' style initialization. Fourth, you will explain the difference between signals and variables inside processes: variables change immediately, useful for intermediate computation, while signals schedule updates after the process. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a milestone so you know when it is verified. Keep these outcomes in mind as you work through examples and the hands-on sequence detector task.

screens.title: Concurrent statements and combinational logic
screens.narratorSegment: Concurrent statements in VHDL model hardware that always evaluates in parallel, mirroring how physical gates and wires behave. A simple concurrent signal assignment like "Y <= A and B;" creates combinational logic that updates whenever any operand changes. This is not a sequential command list; it is a continuous relationship between signals. A common extension is the conditional signal assignment that uses a when-else chain to represent multiplexing: it reads naturally and synthesizes to a tree of selectors. Another form, with-select, provides a compact case-style selection for multiple choices and is syntactically convenient for routing signals based on an index. A key advantage of concurrent forms is clarity: you express the logic relationship and synthesis tools derive the gate network. One misconception is thinking of concurrent assignments as executing in time—rather, they declare continuous relationships. For an example, imagine selecting one of four data inputs based on two select bits; the conditional assignment maps directly to a 4-to-1 multiplexer. Takeaway: use concurrent assignments for pure combinational relationships and prefer conditional or selected forms when mapping multiplexers and decode logic. Concurrent statements and combinational logic means concurrent assignments declare continuous relationships; they synthesize to combinational gates and multiplexers.. In practical terms, how vhdl represents wires and gates using concurrent assignments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Declarative wiring
keyIdea.text: Concurrent assignments declare continuous relationships; they synthesize to combinational gates and multiplexers.

content.html:
Core Concept
Concurrent signal assignments
Declarative expressions that map to combinational hardware. They are evaluated continuously as inputs change and do not represent sequential steps.
  • Conditional signal assignment: readable multiplexer style with when/else chains.
  • Selected signal assignment: compact case-style selection with with ... select.
  • Always ensure the assignment covers all choices to avoid unintended latches.
Example
Y <= A when SEL = "00" else B when SEL = "01" else C when SEL = "10" else D;
Key Takeaway

Prefer concurrent conditional/select assignments to express multiplexers and combinational mapping clearly and synthesizably.

Why this matters
Combinational logic described concurrently is easier to reason about and maps predictably to gates. Simulation shows signals update as soon as inputs change, without waiting for a procedural step.
Common mistake
Using incomplete conditional coverage or mixing sequential intent into concurrent assignments can synthesize latches or create mismatches with simulation.
Pro tip
When designing multiplexers, prefer the selected form for clarity when selecting many cases from a vector selector.

screens.title: Simple concurrent assignment example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a minimal concurrent assignment to make the execution model concrete. The statement "Y <= A and B;" defines a continuous relationship: whenever A or B changes, Y is recomputed and updated. In simulation this behaves like a wire connected to a gate: there is no ordered list of instructions. A common misunderstanding is to think this runs only when a process triggers; instead it is evaluated in parallel. For slightly more complex logic you can chain conditions; for example a two-bit selector that chooses between four inputs is naturally expressed with a when-else chain or a with-select. The example in the code panel shows a conditional assignment selecting A, B, C, or D based on SEL. The important synthesis note is that tools will implement this as a multiplexer tree. For debugging, inspect the waveform: the output name changes as inputs change and there is no clock dependency. Walk away remembering that concurrent statements are your go-to for combinational wiring and pushing selection logic into these forms keeps the design modular and clear. keyIdea.title: Continuous evaluation
keyIdea.text: A single-line concurrent assignment forms a continuously evaluated combinational relationship; use it for gates and multiplexers.

content.html:
Definition
Simple concurrent assignment
A concise way to express combinational gates and direct relationships between signals.
Concrete example
Y <= A and B;  -- updates when A or B changes
This is functionally equivalent to a gate: Y = A & B in other languages. Check waveforms to confirm immediate recomputation.
Example: Conditional select
A readable multiplexer using conditional assignment.
Y <= A when SEL = "00" else  B when SEL = "01" else  C when SEL = "10" else  D;
Misconception
Concurrent is not sequential: do not rely on ordering or process triggers to evaluate these statements.
Check
Run a simulation and toggle SEL and inputs to confirm the output switches immediately without a clock edge.

screens.title: Combinational processes and sensitivity lists
screens.narratorSegment: VHDL processes let you write procedural-style code that still models hardware. A combinational process uses a sensitivity list that contains all inputs the logic depends on; the process runs whenever any listed input changes and computes outputs accordingly. Write the process like a small function: begin with the sensitivity list and then use if or case statements to select outputs. The key rule is to include every signal read within the process in the sensitivity list. If you omit an input the synthesis or simulation may infer a latch, which is often unintended. For example, a multiplexer implemented inside a process should list A, B, C, SEL and any other signals it reads. One benefit of a combinational process is clearer control flow for complicated logic and easier reuse of shared calculations via local variables. A common misconception is treating a combinational process like a clocked one; it is event-driven but not edge-triggered. When you need sequential behavior use a clocked process instead. Takeaway: use full sensitivity lists for combinational processes to ensure transparent synthesis and avoid hidden storage. Combinational processes and sensitivity lists means a combinational process must list every input it reads in the sensitivity list to avoid inferred latches and mismatches between simulation and synthesis.. In practical terms, use processes to form combinational logic when procedural style is clearer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Include all inputs
keyIdea.text: A combinational process must list every input it reads in the sensitivity list to avoid inferred latches and mismatches between simulation and synthesis.

content.html:
Process Flow
Combinational processes
Use processes when procedural clarity is needed; the sensitivity list drives execution.
Example
process (A, B, SEL) begin  if SEL = "00" then   Y <= A;  elsif SEL = "01" then   Y <= B;  else   Y <= D;  end if; end process;
Explanation bullets
  • A process with a full sensitivity list is equivalent to combinational concurrent assignments.
  • Missing an input can create a latch; list every read signal explicitly.
  • Use variables inside the process for intermediate values but remember their immediate update semantics.
Common mistake
Copying a sequential process into combinational context without updating sensitivity lists leads to mismatch between simulation and synthesis.
Key Takeaway

Always keep sensitivity lists complete for combinational processes to avoid unintended storage elements.

screens.title: Sequential processes, rising_edge and synchronous reset
screens.narratorSegment: Sequential behavior in VHDL is modeled inside a clocked process. The pattern you will use most often checks for a clock edge using the function rising_edge(clk). Inside that guarded branch you implement storage updates, including handling synchronous reset and enable signals. For example, when the clock edge occurs, check rst; if asserted, assign q to zeros using vector assignment with others => '0'; else if enable is high then q gets d. The rising_edge function is preferred over older event-based conditions because it explicitly expresses a rising transition and avoids subtle edge detection errors. Remember that within a clocked process signals assigned with <= are updated after the process completes, emulating register behavior. A common error is placing reset handling outside the rising_edge check or using asynchronous constructs unintentionally. For synchronous reset, perform reset inside rising_edge so the reset is applied only on the clock transition. Practice writing a register and observing the waveform: on a rising edge, the old q becomes the newly assigned value shortly after, demonstrating register transfer. Sequential processes, rising_edge and synchronous reset means use rising_edge(clk) to detect clock events and handle synchronous resets inside the same edge branch for predictable register behavior.. In practical terms, implement registers and synchronous reset inside a clocked process. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Clocked register pattern
keyIdea.text: Use rising_edge(clk) to detect clock events and handle synchronous resets inside the same edge branch for predictable register behavior.

content.html:
Process
Clocked process and rising_edge
Sequential updates occur on clock edges; use rising_edge for clarity and safety.
process (clk) begin  if rising_edge(clk) then   if rst = '1' then    q <= (others => '0');   elsif en = '1' then    q <= d;   end if;  end if; end process;
Explanation & tips
  • Place synchronous reset inside rising_edge to have reset sampled by the clock.
  • Use others => '0' to initialize vectors concisely during reset.
  • Signals assigned inside the clocked branch update after the process finishes, modeling registers.
Misconception
Using clk'event and clk = '1' is less explicit and more error prone than rising_edge.
Key Takeaway

Use rising_edge for edge detection and put resets and enables inside the edge branch to create reliable registers.

screens.title: Counters and numeric types
screens.narratorSegment: Counters are a common sequential structure implemented inside a clocked process. The example shows a simple incrementing counter that resets to zero and increments when enabled. A crucial detail for arithmetic is the type you use: arithmetic operators like "+" are defined for numeric types such as unsigned and signed from the IEEE. NUMERIC_STD package. If you declare count as std_logic_vector you cannot directly use the plus operator without conversion, and attempting arithmetic on bit vectors leads to errors or awkward casts. The recommended practice is to declare counters as unsigned and use numeric operations directly, which keeps the code concise and synthesizable. On reset you can assign count '0') to zero all bits. A common misconception is that std_logic_vector is numeric by default; it is not. Another pitfall is relying on overflow behavior without explicit width management. When designing counters, think about wrap-around, width, and whether a saturation or modulo behavior is required. Takeaway: choose the appropriate numeric type to match the operations you intend to perform and make conversions explicit when needed. Counters and numeric types means declare counters as unsigned to use + directly and avoid confusing conversions from std_logic_vector.. In practical terms, why use unsigned instead of std_logic_vector for arithmetic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Type matters
keyIdea.text: Declare counters as unsigned to use + directly and avoid confusing conversions from std_logic_vector.

content.html:
Definition
Counters and numeric types
Use unsigned for arithmetic and initialize with others => '0' during reset.
process (clk) begin  if rising_edge(clk) then   if rst = '1' then    count <= (others => '0');   elsif en = '1' then    count <= count + 1;   end if;  end if; end process;
Explanation
  • Declare count as unsigned to use + without conversions.
  • If you must use std_logic_vector, perform conversions with to_unsigned or to_integer carefully.
  • Decide width based on wrap-around and overflow needs.
Pro tip
Favor numeric types for arithmetic; explicit conversions are clearer and safer for synthesis.

screens.title: Finite State Machines with enumerated types
screens.narratorSegment: Finite state machines in VHDL are robust when you separate the state register from the next-state combinational logic. First, define an enumerated type listing the states, for example type state_type is (GREEN, YELLOW, RED); then declare signals state and next_state of that type. Implement the state register as a clocked process: on rising_edge(clk) write state <= GREEN when reset, else state <= next_state. Implement next-state logic in a separate combinational process that lists state and any inputs like timer_done. Inside that process use a case statement with when clauses to set next_state based on conditions. Using enumerated types makes the code self-documenting and simulation-friendly: many tools will show state names in waveforms rather than binary encodings. A common misconception is that enumerations add overhead; synthesis tools typically encode them efficiently. The separation also prevents accidental mixing of sequential and combinational behavior and improves testability. Takeaway: prefer enumeration and two-process FSM structure for readable, maintainable, and synthesizable state machines. Finite State Machines with enumerated types means use an enumerated state type, a clocked state register, and a separate combinational next-state process for clear fsm design.. In practical terms, separate state register and next-state logic for clarity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two-process FSM
keyIdea.text: Use an enumerated state type, a clocked state register, and a separate combinational next-state process for clear FSM design.

content.html:
Architecture
FSM pattern with enumeration
Define states with an enum and split register and next-state logic for clarity and simulation friendliness.
Example types
type state_type is (GREEN, YELLOW, RED); signal state, next_state : state_type;
Next-state process
List state and inputs in the sensitivity list and use case statements to assign next_state.
process (state, timer_done) begin  case state is   when GREEN =>    if timer_done = '1' then next_state <= YELLOW; else next_state <= GREEN;    end if;   when others =>    next_state <= GREEN;  end case; end process;
Why enumerate?
Enumerated states improve readability, allow named states in waveforms, and let synthesis assign efficient encodings automatically.

screens.title: Signals vs Variables inside processes
screens.narratorSegment: Inside a process you can use both signals and variables, but they have different timing semantics and roles. A variable is updated immediately when you assign to it; subsequent lines in the same process see the updated value. Variables are local to the process and are useful for intermediate calculations, loop indices, or building a value before assigning it to a signal. A signal, by contrast, schedules its new value and the actual update becomes visible only after the process suspends; this models a non-blocking or deferred update and represents physical wiring or storage. A common example: inside a clocked process you may compute an intermediate sum into a variable and then assign that variable to a signal at the end; the simulation shows the signal change after the process completes. A frequent mistake is assuming signals update immediately and writing code that mistakenly depends on signal mutation within the same process. When designing synthesizable code, use variables for temporary combinational work and signals for registers and inter-process communication. Takeaway: remember "variable now, signal later" when reasoning about updates inside processes.

keyIdea.title: Timing difference
keyIdea.text: Variables update immediately inside a process; signals schedule updates at process end — use variables for local computation and signals for storage/communication.

content.html:
Definition
Signals vs Variables
Different update timing and scope make each appropriate for different tasks inside a process.
process (clk) variable temp : unsigned(7 downto 0); begin  if rising_edge(clk) then   temp := a + b;   sum <= temp;  end if; end process;
Here temp updates immediately and sum is scheduled, matching register behavior at the process boundary.
Explanation & pitfalls
  • Use variables for intermediate calculations where immediate feedback matters inside the process.
  • Avoid expecting signals to have their new value until after the process completes; this leads to logic bugs.
  • Signals create visible communication across processes and must be used for registers and outputs.
Common mistake
Confusing variable and signal timing inside a clocked process and relying on immediate signal changes within the same process.

screens.title: VHDL selected/conditional vs process implementations
screens.narratorSegment: There are often two ways to express the same combinational function in VHDL: as a concurrent selected or conditional assignment, or inside a combinational process. The concurrent forms are concise and map directly to multiplexers, making them easy to read when the logic is primarily selection of inputs. The combinational process is preferable when you have more complex control flow, multiple dependent calculations, or need local variables for intermediate results. For example, a multi-stage selection with computed indices might be clearer in a process, while straightforward routing based on a selector is cleaner with with-select. A useful workflow is to start with concurrent constructs for simple mapping and switch to a process when clarity or reuse of temporary values becomes important. A misconception is to prefer processes exclusively because they look like software; processes can be used appropriately but require careful sensitivity list management. Takeaway: choose the simplest concurrent form for pure selection; choose a process when procedural clarity, intermediate variables, or complex case analysis is needed. Comparison
Concurrent select vs Process
Use concurrent when logic is direct selection; use process when control flow or intermediate steps are needed.
Concurrent example
with SEL select Y <= A when "00", B when "01", C when "10", D when others;
Process example
process (SEL, A, B, C) begin case SEL is when "00" => Y <= A; when others => Y <= D; end case; end process;
Practical guidance

screens.title: VHDL vs Verilog: FSM readability and waveform names
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing VHDL and Verilog for FSMs highlights trade-offs in readability and simulation presentation. VHDL enumerated types allow you to name states directly and many simulators will display the state signal as text labels, for example GREEN, YELLOW, RED, instead of binary encodings. This improves human comprehension when inspecting waveforms. Verilog often uses numeric encodings for states, which requires mapping numbers to names mentally or with comments. From a synthesis point of view both approaches produce similar hardware because enumerations are encoded as binary by the tool. However, in design and debugging, VHDL's explicit enumerations and the two-process FSM style make intent clearer and reduce errors. One caution is not to assume enumerations eliminate the need to think about encoding width or synthesis options; they simply provide abstraction and readability. As a practical exercise, implement the same FSM in both languages and compare the waveform: note whether you can read state transitions directly and how that affected your debugging speed. Takeaway: prefer enumeration for readability, especially during simulation and debugging. screens.title: Common pitfalls and verification checks
screens.narratorSegment: Before concluding, let's collect common pitfalls and verification checks you should perform. First, incomplete conditional coverage or missing sensitivity list entries often lead to inferred latches. The verification check is straightforward: simulate with multiple input patterns and look for signals that hold state unexpectedly when inputs change. Second, using std_logic_vector for arithmetic without explicit conversions can hide bugs; verify arithmetic using unsigned or signed types or perform controlled casts. Third, placing reset handling outside of rising_edge leads to asynchronous behavior; decide whether you need synchronous or asynchronous reset and implement accordingly, then observe the waveform to confirm the reset timing. Fourth, confusing signals and variables inside a process will result in surprising immediate versus deferred updates; test small process snippets to see the difference. For each check, write short targeted tests in your testbench that toggle signals and examine waveforms for the expected update timing. Takeaway: pair disciplined VHDL styles with focused simulation checks to catch these typical mistakes early. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn the two fundamental ways VHDL models hardware: concurrent statements that behave like physical wires and sequential statements inside processes that behave like small programs driven by events. You will see how simple concurrent signal assignments map directly to combinational gates, how conditional and selected assignments express multiplexing cleanly, and how processes use sensitivity lists and clock-edge checks to implement registers and finite state machines. We will practice counters, synchronous reset patterns, and a state-machine design that uses an enumerated type for readable states. You will also observe the important difference between signals and variables inside a process: signals update after the process completes, while variables update immediately and are useful for temporary calculations. These patterns are essential for synthesizable, maintainable HDL. By the end you'll be able to choose the correct VHDL construct for combinational logic versus sequential logic and reason about timing and synthesis implications. Think about a design you might write: will the behavior be expressed as parallel wiring or as time-driven state updates?

These objectives map to practical VHDL skills you will practice. First, you will use concurrent signal assignments and the conditional select forms to express combinational logic concisely and in a way that synthesizes to gates and multiplexers. For example, you will write a conditional assignment that selects one of four inputs based on a two-bit selector. Second, you will write processes with full sensitivity lists to model combinational behavior and understand why listing every input matters. This helps avoid accidental latches and ensures predictable synthesis. Third, you will implement registers, counters, and finite state machines with clock-edge detection and synchronous reset patterns so your design updates only on clock edges. You will code a counter that increments under enable and resets with others => '0' style initialization. Fourth, you will explain the difference between signals and variables inside processes: variables change immediately, useful for intermediate computation, while signals schedule updates after the process. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a milestone so you know when it is verified. Keep these outcomes in mind as you work through examples and the hands-on sequence detector task.

This second objectives slide frames the hands-on evidence you'll produce. You will implement a 4-bit counter with enable and synchronous reset and verify that the counter increments only on clock edges and resets to zeros when reset is asserted. You will also implement an FSM using an enumerated type and write a simple testbench that steps the input sequence to validate next-state transitions. These exercises demonstrate comprehension of synthesis constraints: for arithmetic use unsigned types or proper conversions, and for state machines prefer enumeration for readability. Finally, you will perform a short code review to identify where a missing sensitivity list could create a latch and where a variable inside a process must not be assumed to represent storage. Each task ends with a short check: does the waveform show the state names and do signals update only after the clock event? These verification steps tie coding style to observable timing behavior in simulation.

Concurrent statements in VHDL model hardware that always evaluates in parallel, mirroring how physical gates and wires behave. A simple concurrent signal assignment like "Y <= A and B;" creates combinational logic that updates whenever any operand changes. This is not a sequential command list; it is a continuous relationship between signals. A common extension is the conditional signal assignment that uses a when-else chain to represent multiplexing: it reads naturally and synthesizes to a tree of selectors. Another form, with-select, provides a compact case-style selection for multiple choices and is syntactically convenient for routing signals based on an index. A key advantage of concurrent forms is clarity: you express the logic relationship and synthesis tools derive the gate network. One misconception is thinking of concurrent assignments as executing in time—rather, they declare continuous relationships. For an example, imagine selecting one of four data inputs based on two select bits; the conditional assignment maps directly to a 4-to-1 multiplexer. Takeaway: use concurrent assignments for pure combinational relationships and prefer conditional or selected forms when mapping multiplexers and decode logic. Concurrent statements and combinational logic means concurrent assignments declare continuous relationships; they synthesize to combinational gates and multiplexers.. In practical terms, how vhdl represents wires and gates using concurrent assignments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a minimal concurrent assignment to make the execution model concrete. The statement "Y <= A and B;" defines a continuous relationship: whenever A or B changes, Y is recomputed and updated. In simulation this behaves like a wire connected to a gate: there is no ordered list of instructions. A common misunderstanding is to think this runs only when a process triggers; instead it is evaluated in parallel. For slightly more complex logic you can chain conditions; for example a two-bit selector that chooses between four inputs is naturally expressed with a when-else chain or a with-select. The example in the code panel shows a conditional assignment selecting A, B, C, or D based on SEL. The important synthesis note is that tools will implement this as a multiplexer tree. For debugging, inspect the waveform: the output name changes as inputs change and there is no clock dependency. Walk away remembering that concurrent statements are your go-to for combinational wiring and pushing selection logic into these forms keeps the design modular and clear. Simple concurrent assignment example means a single-line concurrent assignment forms a continuously evaluated combinational relationship; use it for gates and multiplexers.. In practical terms, from logical and to combinational sensitivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

VHDL processes let you write procedural-style code that still models hardware. A combinational process uses a sensitivity list that contains all inputs the logic depends on; the process runs whenever any listed input changes and computes outputs accordingly. Write the process like a small function: begin with the sensitivity list and then use if or case statements to select outputs. The key rule is to include every signal read within the process in the sensitivity list. If you omit an input the synthesis or simulation may infer a latch, which is often unintended. For example, a multiplexer implemented inside a process should list A, B, C, SEL and any other signals it reads. One benefit of a combinational process is clearer control flow for complicated logic and easier reuse of shared calculations via local variables. A common misconception is treating a combinational process like a clocked one; it is event-driven but not edge-triggered. When you need sequential behavior use a clocked process instead. Takeaway: use full sensitivity lists for combinational processes to ensure transparent synthesis and avoid hidden storage. Combinational processes and sensitivity lists means a combinational process must list every input it reads in the sensitivity list to avoid inferred latches and mismatches between simulation and synthesis.. In practical terms, use processes to form combinational logic when procedural style is clearer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Sequential behavior in VHDL is modeled inside a clocked process. The pattern you will use most often checks for a clock edge using the function rising_edge(clk). Inside that guarded branch you implement storage updates, including handling synchronous reset and enable signals. For example, when the clock edge occurs, check rst; if asserted, assign q to zeros using vector assignment with others => '0'; else if enable is high then q gets d. The rising_edge function is preferred over older event-based conditions because it explicitly expresses a rising transition and avoids subtle edge detection errors. Remember that within a clocked process signals assigned with <= are updated after the process completes, emulating register behavior. A common error is placing reset handling outside the rising_edge check or using asynchronous constructs unintentionally. For synchronous reset, perform reset inside rising_edge so the reset is applied only on the clock transition. Practice writing a register and observing the waveform: on a rising edge, the old q becomes the newly assigned value shortly after, demonstrating register transfer. Sequential processes, rising_edge and synchronous reset means use rising_edge(clk) to detect clock events and handle synchronous resets inside the same edge branch for predictable register behavior.. In practical terms, implement registers and synchronous reset inside a clocked process. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Inside a process you can use both signals and variables, but they have different timing semantics and roles. A variable is updated immediately when you assign to it; subsequent lines in the same process see the updated value. Variables are local to the process and are useful for intermediate calculations, loop indices, or building a value before assigning it to a signal. A signal, by contrast, schedules its new value and the actual update becomes visible only after the process suspends; this models a non-blocking or deferred update and represents physical wiring or storage. A common example: inside a clocked process you may compute an intermediate sum into a variable and then assign that variable to a signal at the end; the simulation shows the signal change after the process completes. A frequent mistake is assuming signals update immediately and writing code that mistakenly depends on signal mutation within the same process. When designing synthesizable code, use variables for temporary combinational work and signals for registers and inter-process communication. Takeaway: remember "variable now, signal later" when reasoning about updates inside processes.

The concurrent forms are concise and map directly to multiplexers, making them easy to read when the logic is primarily selection of inputs. The combinational process is preferable when you have more complex control flow, multiple dependent calculations, or need local variables for intermediate results. For example, a multi-stage selection with computed indices might be clearer in a process, while straightforward routing based on a selector is cleaner with with-select. A useful workflow is to start with concurrent constructs for simple mapping and switch to a process when clarity or reuse of temporary values becomes important.
